article.title: September PPI: energy drove the goods surge as services rose
article.dek: The BLS release of 15 October 2026 showed a 1.3% September headline rise and a 0.5% increase excluding foods, energy and trade services. The component detail separates the energy shock from wider monthly gains.
article.search_title: September 2026 PPI: energy, services and underlying inflation
article.meta_description: September 2026 PPI rose 1.3%. Examine energy, services and underlying gains in the 15 October BLS release, with two years of first-reported changes.
article.social_hook: September 2026 PPI retrospective: energy drove the goods surge, while services and the underlying measure rose too.
article.substack_body_markdown:
The September 2026 Producer Price Index combined a 1.3% monthly headline increase with a 0.5% rise excluding foods, energy and trade services, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics release of 15 October 2026. Energy dominated the increase in goods prices, while services rose too. The question is how much of that pressure extended beyond the biggest commodity move. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

Our reading is that the component mix deserves as much attention as the headline. September showed positive price changes across several categories, but the size of the energy jump makes it especially important to separate a one-month shock from evidence of persistence. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

## September's jump was broad, but uneven

Final demand goods rose 2.6% in September and services rose 0.8%. The measure excluding foods, energy and trade services increased 0.5%, following 0.3% in August as stated in the September release. All these monthly rates are seasonally adjusted. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

The underlying measure is a separate view of the same price system, with those categories excluded. It overlaps the goods and services aggregates; its rate is not an extra contribution to add to them. The comparison shows both the goods surge and the smaller gains that remained after the exclusions. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

## How September compares with two years of first releases

The history chart follows the monthly changes as first reported in dated BLS releases, from October 2024 through September 2026. On that basis, September's 1.3% headline increase was below April 2026's 1.4%. The underlying measure also varied across the period: its September increase of 0.5% was below May 2026's first-reported 0.8%. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_2]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

That history differs from a chart rewritten with later revisions. August headline PPI was first reported at 0.4%; the September release revised it to 0.5%. July was initially unchanged and stood at 0.2% in the September release. Thus the September-release comparison is 1.3% after 0.5%, while the first-release chart preserves the earlier observations. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_2]]

## Energy and trade margins explain the split

In the September 2026 release, BLS attributed over 80% of the goods increase to energy, which rose 10.8%. Services prices also rose 0.8%. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

Within goods, foods rose 1.2% and the index excluding foods and energy rose 0.3%. Those figures explain why a strong goods total need not mean similarly large price increases in every goods category. The energy share cited by BLS describes the goods increase, not the entire final-demand increase. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

Services had their own composition. Trade-service margins rose 1.4%, accounting for nearly half of the services increase, according to BLS. Transportation and warehousing services rose 3.4%, while services excluding trade, transportation and warehousing rose 0.3%. Trade services here refer to margins, a distinction that matters when interpreting that category. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

The component chart compares each category's own monthly rate. It is not a contribution waterfall: adding these rates, or treating the energy rate as a percentage-point contribution to headline inflation, would misread the figures. The services detail provides a separate check on the idea that September was exclusively an energy story. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

## The limits of a one-month signal

The September 2026 countercase is concentration: goods excluding foods and energy rose 0.3%, and services excluding trade, transportation and warehousing also rose 0.3%. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

Those narrower gains were positive, yet much smaller than the energy increase. That is the strongest reason to resist treating the headline pace as representative of every component or extrapolating it as a continuing monthly rate. The release supports a distinction between concentrated strength and the smaller increases elsewhere. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

A lasting inflation signal from the September 2026 release would require repeated gains outside energy; weaker underlying readings would challenge it. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

That is a test for an interpretation, rather than a forecast supplied by this release. These producer-price observations alone do not establish a consumer-inflation outcome or an automatic Federal Reserve response. The unresolved issue is whether pressure beyond energy persists, not whether the largest monthly number can stand in for the whole report. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

Retrospective analysis, written on 5 November 2026 (GMT+7). This article examines the September PPI release of 15 October 2026 and earlier dated releases. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_2]] [[SOURCE:SOURCE_3]]

Analysis, not financial advice. Readers decide whether to trade. [[SOURCE:SOURCE_1]]

visual_editorial_decision.countercase: Energy rose 10.8%, while goods excluding foods and energy and services excluding trade, transportation and warehousing each rose 0.3%. The goods shock was highly concentrated, and one positive underlying monthly reading cannot establish persistence. Trade-service prices measure margins. The 24-month first-release history also shows volatility: September's 1.3% headline first print was below April 2026's 1.4%, so do not call it the largest rise in that window.
visual_editorial_decision.editorial_thesis: The September release combined a 1.3% monthly headline PPI rise with a 2.6% increase in goods, a 0.8% rise in services and a 0.5% rise excluding foods, energy and trade services. Energy dominated the goods increase, according to BLS, while the services and underlying measures show why an energy-only reading is incomplete. This is a dated analysis of the 15 October 2026 release; the visual argument does not extrapolate one month into a consumer-inflation or Federal Reserve forecast.

material_claim_bindings.claim_text: September PPI: energy drove the goods surge as services rose
material_claim_bindings.support_excerpt: Final demand goods: Prices for final demand goods advanced 2.6 percent in September, the largest increase since data were first calculated in December 2009. Over 80 percent of the broad-based rise in September is attributable to the index for final demand energy, which jumped 10.8 percent. Prices for final demand foods and for final demand goods less foods and energy advanced 1.2 percent and 0.3 percent, respectively. Product detail: Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent. The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7 percent. The indexes for thermoplastic resins and materials and for commercial electric power also declined. (See table 2.) Final demand services: Prices for final demand services moved up 0.8 percent in September, the largest rise since advancing 0.8 percent in April. Nearly half of the broad-based September increase can be attributed to a 1.4-percent rise in margins for final demand trade services. The indexes for final demand transportation and warehousing services and for final demand services less trade, transportation, and warehousing also advanced, 3.4 percent and 0.3 percent, respectively.
